metadata.title: Leg Weave Bottom Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Leg Weave Bottom in BJJ. Defensive half guard position with 35% escape rate. Complete guide covering frames, escapes, and defensive strategies.

overview: Leg Weave Bottom Position represents a challenging defensive scenario in half guard where the top player has threaded their leg through your half guard structure, establishing a powerful passing position. This position occurs when the passer has successfully weaved their knee-side leg between your legs while maintaining upper body control, creating significant pressure and limiting your mobility. The bottom player faces immediate threats of guard passes to side control, mount, or back control if defensive frames and hip movement are not properly established. While disadvantageous, this position offers specific defensive pathways and counter-attacks that can recover guard or create scrambles when executed with proper timing and technique. Understanding the mechanics of maintaining frames, creating angles, and preventing the complete pass is essential for survival and eventual escape from this high-pressure position.
state_invariants: Top player's knee-side leg is threaded between bottom player's legs, typically positioning the shin or knee across the bottom player's hip line or thigh to establish the weave structure
Bottom player maintains half guard hook with one leg (usually the far leg) while the near leg is being controlled or pressured by the top player's weaved leg
Top player applies forward and downward pressure through chest and shoulder, often with crossface or underhook control to flatten the bottom player
Bottom player's back is on or near the mat with varying degrees of hip escape and shoulder rotation depending on defensive frame effectiveness
Space between players is minimal due to the leg weave creating tight connection, requiring bottom player to actively create frames with forearms, elbows, or knees
prerequisites: Bottom player was in half guard position (standard, knee shield, or lockdown variation)
Top player successfully initiated leg weave entry by threading knee-side leg between bottom player's legs
Bottom player failed to prevent the initial weave with knee shield or frame
Top player established some form of upper body control (crossface, underhook, or collar tie)
Bottom player's far-side leg maintains some connection (half guard hook) preventing complete pass
key_principles: Establish and maintain strong defensive frames using forearms against opponent's neck, shoulder, or hip to prevent complete flattening
Keep active hip movement and angle creation to prevent top player from settling their weight and consolidating position
Protect the underhook battle - fight to maintain or recover underhook on the near side to limit top player's control
Use far-side leg (hook) actively to disrupt balance and prevent top player from stepping over or completing passes
Create space through bridging and shrimping movements to insert knee shield or recover full guard structure
Monitor and defend crossface pressure - prevent head control which enables easier passing sequences
Maintain awareness of back exposure - avoid turning too far into opponent when attempting escapes

counter_transitions.trigger: Top player attempts to flatten with crossface - create frame on neck and shrimp hip away
Top player drives forward pressure - dive under their center of gravity to deep half
Top player posts hands forward - capture underhook and roll to top
Top player elevates to complete pass - come up on elbow to seated position

decision_tree.condition: If top player establishes strong crossface and drives chest pressure to flatten you
If top player posts hands forward or elevates hips to step over your leg
If top player drives weight forward while maintaining low posture
If top player attempts to free their leg from your hook while controlling upper body

common_errors.error: Allowing top player to establish deep crossface without fighting for frames
common_errors.consequence: Complete flattening occurs, eliminating hip mobility and making escapes extremely difficult. Top player can consolidate position and pass at will.
common_errors.correction: Immediately establish forearm or elbow frame against opponent's neck or shoulder as leg weave begins. Keep active resistance to prevent head control. Prioritize frame maintenance over other defensive actions initially.

common_errors.error: Releasing far-side leg hook prematurely in attempt to escape
common_errors.consequence: Top player completes pass immediately to side control or mount without resistance. Loss of only remaining connection point accelerates positional loss.
common_errors.correction: Maintain far-side hook throughout escape attempts unless deliberately transitioning to deep half or other guard recovery. Use hook to off-balance opponent and create scramble opportunities. Only release when secured alternative position.

common_errors.error: Remaining static and accepting the position without hip movement
common_errors.consequence: Top player settles weight and consolidates leg weave, making escape progressively more difficult. Energy depletes while defending without attempting improvement.
common_errors.correction: Keep constant hip movement even if small - shrimp, bridge, angle changes. Never accept static position. Create micro-adjustments that prevent opponent from settling and set up larger escape movements.

common_errors.error: Turning fully into opponent to escape, exposing back
common_errors.consequence: Top player takes back control or achieves crucifix position. What began as guard pass defense becomes back attack defense with worse odds.
common_errors.correction: Maintain awareness of back exposure threshold. When turning to dogfight or deep half, keep shoulders within 45 degrees of mat. If forced further, transition to turtle with defensive posture rather than giving up back mount.

common_errors.error: Using only upper body strength to fight frames without hip engagement
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue quickly while top player maintains pressure through better leverage. Frame battle is lost leading to flattening and pass.
common_errors.correction: Coordinate frame pressure with hip movement and leg engagement. Use shrimping motion to create angle that makes frames more effective. Engage core and legs to support arm frames rather than isolated upper body pushing.

common_errors.error: Attempting deep half entry without proper angle or timing
common_errors.consequence: Top player sprawls weight back, crushes the attempted entry, and often transitions to more dominant positions like north-south or back control.
common_errors.correction: Only shoot deep half when opponent drives forward pressure or posts hands. Create angle first with frame and shrimp to position hips. Time entry when opponent's weight is committed forward, making sprawl defense impossible.

training_drills.name: Leg Weave Escape Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Partner establishes leg weave with moderate pressure. Bottom player cycles through frame creation, hip escape, knee shield recovery, and dogfight entries for 2-minute rounds. Top player maintains position but allows escapes to complete, then re-establishes weave. Focus on smooth transitions between defensive options.

training_drills.name: Progressive Resistance Leg Weave Defense
training_drills.description: Start with compliant top player allowing bottom player to work all escape options. Gradually increase resistance over 5 rounds: 30% resistance, 50%, 70%, 90%, then 100% competitive. Bottom player maintains same escape attempts throughout increasing difficulty. Identifies which escapes work under pressure.
training_drills.duration: 5 rounds of 3 minutes with increasing resistance

training_drills.name: Frame Maintenance Under Pressure
training_drills.description: Top player establishes leg weave and applies sustained crossface and chest pressure for 30-second intervals. Bottom player focuses solely on maintaining strong frames without attempting escapes. Develop frame endurance and proper positioning under realistic pressure. Rest 30 seconds between intervals.
training_drills.duration: 10 intervals of 30 seconds on, 30 seconds rest

training_drills.name: Leg Weave to Deep Half Timing Drill
training_drills.description: Top player alternates between forward pressure and backward weight shifts. Bottom player identifies windows for deep half entry based on weight distribution. Practice shooting deep half only when opponent commits weight forward. Develops timing recognition and entry precision.

training_drills.name: Leg Weave Positional Sparring
training_drills.description: Start every round in leg weave bottom position. Bottom player scores by recovering guard, sweeping, or escaping. Top player scores by passing to side control or better. Reset to leg weave after each score. Competitive environment to test all defensive options under pressure.

expert_insights.danaher: The leg weave bottom position represents a critical junction in the half guard passing sequence where the battle of angles and frames determines outcome. The fundamental principle at work here is the concept of inside position versus outside position - the top player has achieved inside leg positioning through the weave, creating a biomechanical advantage that must be neutralized through superior frame construction and hip angle management. The key defensive insight is that frames are not static structures but dynamic tools that create distance, which then enables angle creation through shrimping mechanics. Most bottom players make the catastrophic error of accepting the flat position, at which point the passer's weight advantage becomes insurmountable. The intelligent escape sequence begins with establishing frames that prevent complete chest-to-chest contact, then immediately creating hip angle to insert the knee shield or transition to deep half guard. Understanding that this position is fundamentally about the battle for inside control - once lost with the leg weave, it must be systematically recovered through precise technical sequences rather than explosive scrambling.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Leg weave bottom is honestly one of the worst positions to be in during competition because good passers will flatten you and pass in seconds if you don't know the specific escapes. From my experience at the highest levels, the absolute key is never letting them settle their weight - you need to be moving your hips constantly even if it's small movements. The frame on the neck is non-negotiable, that's your survival tool that buys you time to hip escape. What works for me when I end up here is immediately recognizing whether they're driving forward pressure or trying to step over - if they drive forward, that's your deep half window, if they elevate to step over, that's when you come up to dogfight. Against elite guys like Lachlan Giles or Nick Rodriguez who have incredible pressure, I've found that the old school sweep becomes viable because they commit so much weight forward trying to flatten you. The biggest mistake I see is people giving up the position mentally and just accepting the pass - if you keep fighting for frames and angles, you'd be surprised how many scrambles you can create even against world-class passers.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The leg weave is basically the passer trying to kill your lockdown and half guard game, but there's some sick counters if you know the 10th Planet system. First thing, don't let them flatten you bro - that's death. You gotta keep that electric chair option alive by maintaining your leg connection and looking for that ankle. A lot of people don't realize that when they weave their leg through, they're actually giving you a potential path to the twister side control if you can get the underhook and roll them. The deep half entry is money here too, especially if you've been drilling the dogfight to deep half connection. What I teach is to always be thinking about the lockdown recovery even from bad positions like this - if you can get your foot across their hip while they're weaving, you can sometimes trap their leg and create the whole lockdown game again. The vaporizer sweep is also there if they commit too much weight forward and you have that far leg hook. Bottom line is leg weave bottom is dangerous but it's not game over - you've got electric chair, deep half, dogfight, and if you're flexible enough, rubber guard entries when they post their hands. Keep moving, maintain that hook, and look for the counters.

metadata.title: Leg Weave Position Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Leg Weave Position Top in BJJ. Advanced guard passing position with leg control and weight distribution. Success rates: Beginner 35%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.

overview:
Leg Weave Position Top is an advanced guard passing position where the top practitioner weaves their leg between the bottom player's legs to establish control and weight distribution. This position is most commonly used when passing half guard or dealing with stubborn leg retention from the bottom player. The weaving action creates a unique mechanical advantage that disrupts the bottom player's defensive structure while establishing a dominant passing angle.

The position is characterized by threading one leg through the opponent's guard, typically while maintaining upper body control through underhooks, crossface, or grip control. This creates a powerful pressure-passing platform where the top player can distribute their weight effectively across the opponent's defensive frames. The leg weave disrupts common half guard retention strategies and eliminates the bottom player's ability to effectively use butterfly hooks or knee shields.

Leg Weave Position Top is particularly effective in modern no-gi grappling where traditional gi grips are unavailable, forcing practitioners to rely more heavily on positional mechanics and weight distribution. The position requires good hip mobility and precise weight placement to prevent the bottom player from re-establishing their guard structure.
state_invariants: Top player's leg threaded between opponent's legs, creating a weaving pattern that disrupts the bottom player's defensive frame and prevents hip mobility
Top player's chest and shoulder pressure directed toward opponent's upper body, typically through crossface or shoulder-of-justice positioning with sustained forward pressure
Bottom player's guard structure compromised, with limited ability to create frames or maintain distance due to the leg weaving action controlling hip movement
Top player maintains low base with hips driving forward, weight distributed through the woven leg and upper body pressure points to prevent bottom player recovery
prerequisites: Successful entry from half guard passing sequence or knee slice attempt
Control of opponent's upper body through underhook, crossface, or shoulder pressure
One leg threaded between opponent's legs in weaving position
Opponent's guard structure disrupted with limited ability to retain hooks or frames
Top player maintaining forward pressure and low center of gravity
Bottom player flat on back or defensive position with compromised leg retention
key_principles: Maintain constant forward pressure through chest and shoulder, never allowing opponent to create space or recover guard structure
Keep weaving leg active and mobile to prevent opponent from establishing hooks or controlling the leg
Distribute weight strategically between upper body pressure and leg positioning to maximize control
Control opponent's near-side arm through underhook or wrist control to prevent defensive frames
Use crossface or shoulder pressure to control opponent's head and limit their mobility options
Keep hips low and driving forward to prevent opponent from creating space underneath
Anticipate opponent's attempts to recover guard and preemptively adjust weight distribution

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to create frames or turn into you
Opponent exposes underhook side while defending leg weave
Opponent's legs become extended or disconnected during recovery attempt
Opponent turns away to escape pressure and exposes back
Opponent flattens out and loses hip mobility

decision_tree.condition: If opponent maintains strong knee shield or creates frames to prevent forward progress
If opponent turns into you and exposes underhook or attempts deep half entry
If opponent flattens out and loses hip mobility while defending
If opponent turns away to escape pressure and exposes their back
Else if opponent maintains defensive posture but cannot escape

common_errors.error: Rising too high with hips during leg weave, reducing pressure and allowing opponent to create space
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can shrimp away, recover guard structure, or insert knee shield to prevent pass completion
common_errors.correction: Maintain low hip position with chest driving forward, keeping weight distributed through shoulder and weaving leg to maximize pressure

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's near-side arm, allowing them to create defensive frames
common_errors.consequence: Opponent establishes strong frames that prevent forward progress and create opportunities for guard recovery or sweeps
common_errors.correction: Secure underhook or wrist control on near-side arm immediately, using crossface or shoulder pressure to pin arm and eliminate framing opportunities

common_errors.error: Leaving weaving leg static and vulnerable to opponent's leg control or entanglement
common_errors.consequence: Opponent captures weaving leg with lockdown, butterfly hook, or other leg retention that stalls pass and creates sweep opportunities
common_errors.correction: Keep weaving leg active and mobile, constantly adjusting position to prevent opponent from establishing hooks or controlling the leg

common_errors.error: Committing too much weight to one side without proper balance, making position unstable
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can use your imbalanced weight distribution to create sweep opportunities or recover guard easily
common_errors.correction: Distribute weight strategically between upper body pressure and leg positioning, maintaining active balance and ability to adjust

common_errors.error: Neglecting head control and allowing opponent freedom of movement with their upper body
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can turn into you, create angles for sweeps, or establish grips that compromise your passing control
common_errors.correction: Use crossface, shoulder-of-justice, or head control to limit opponent's mobility and prevent them from turning or creating favorable angles

common_errors.error: Rushing the pass without establishing proper control points first
common_errors.consequence: Opponent exploits gaps in your control to recover guard, execute sweeps, or create scrambles that negate your passing advantage
common_errors.correction: Establish solid control through upper body pressure, arm control, and leg positioning before attempting to complete the pass to side control

common_errors.error: Failing to anticipate opponent's common defensive reactions like knee shield insertion or deep half attempts
common_errors.consequence: Opponent successfully defends and recovers guard structure, forcing you to restart the passing sequence from a less advantageous position
common_errors.correction: Read opponent's defensive patterns and preemptively adjust weight and positioning to counter their most likely defensive responses before they can execute them

training_drills.name: Leg Weave Entry Repetitions
training_drills.description: Partner starts in half guard bottom with standard retention. Top player practices threading leg and establishing weave position, focusing on smooth entry mechanics and immediate pressure establishment. Reset and repeat 10-15 times per side.

training_drills.name: Pressure Maintenance Drill
training_drills.description: Start in established leg weave position. Bottom player uses 50% resistance to create frames and attempt guard recovery. Top player focuses on maintaining constant pressure, controlling arms, and preventing space creation. Hold position for 2 minutes, then switch.

training_drills.name: Weave to Pass Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Top player enters leg weave position and flows through various passing options (knee slice, smash pass, long step) based on bottom player's defensive reactions. Bottom player provides realistic but controlled resistance. Focus on reading reactions and selecting appropriate passing technique.

training_drills.name: Counter Defense Drill
training_drills.description: Bottom player attempts specific escapes (deep half, knee shield recovery, underhook sweep) from leg weave position. Top player practices recognizing and countering each escape attempt with appropriate passing adjustments. Work through 5-6 common escape scenarios.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Leg Weave
training_drills.description: Start in leg weave position with full resistance. Top player attempts to complete pass to side control or mount. Bottom player attempts to recover full guard or sweep. Reset when position is achieved by either player. 3-minute rounds.

expert_insights.danaher: The leg weave position represents a sophisticated mechanical solution to the problem of stubborn half guard retention. By threading your leg through the opponent's defensive structure, you create a pressure angle that is biomechanically difficult to defend against. The key insight is that the weaving action disrupts the opponent's ability to generate hip power, which is the foundation of all guard retention. When executed properly, the leg weave transforms a dynamic guard passing exchange into a controlled pressure scenario where you dictate the pace and direction of the engagement. The position requires precise weight distribution—too much weight on the legs and you lose upper body control; too much on the upper body and your legs become vulnerable to entanglement. Master practitioners understand that the leg weave is not merely a passing position but a control platform from which multiple passing paths become available based on the opponent's defensive reactions.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Leg weave is one of my most reliable positions for passing stubborn half guard players in competition, especially against opponents who are good at maintaining knee shields and creating frames. The beauty of this position is that it gives you dominant control while maintaining multiple passing options based on how your opponent reacts. In high-level competition, most opponents will try to turn into you or establish deep half when you establish the leg weave—this is exactly what you want because it opens up darce and anaconda opportunities while they're trying to escape the pressure. The mistake most people make is trying to force the pass too quickly instead of using the position to break down the opponent's defensive structure first. I like to establish heavy shoulder pressure and control their near arm, then wait for them to make a defensive move that creates an opening. Against elite competition, the leg weave also sets up excellent transitions to the truck position if they turn away, giving you back attack opportunities.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The leg weave is a fascinating position because it challenges conventional passing wisdom by intentionally putting your leg in a potentially vulnerable position. From the 10th Planet perspective, we see this as a high-risk, high-reward scenario that forces both players into dynamic problem-solving. What makes leg weave interesting is how it interacts with our lockdown-based half guard system—when someone tries to leg weave against a skilled lockdown player, it can backfire spectacularly if they don't understand the counters. That said, when executed by someone who really understands the mechanics, leg weave can be brutally effective because it disrupts the bottom player's ability to generate the hip movement necessary for most modern half guard attacks. The innovative approach is to combine leg weave with different upper body control variations—crossface, underhook, whizzer control—creating different pressure patterns that the opponent has to solve. I teach students to think of leg weave not as a single technique but as a pressure framework that adapts to the opponent's defensive strategy.

metadata.title: Leg Weave Top Position | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Leg Weave Top Position in BJJ. Advanced guard passing control with leg entanglement. Complete guide with 70% pass completion rate for advanced practitioners.

overview:
The Leg Weave Top Position is an advanced guard passing control where the top player threads one leg between the bottom player's legs while maintaining upper body control. This position creates a powerful passing platform by neutralizing the bottom player's leg-based guards and frames. The leg weave is particularly effective against opponents who rely heavily on knee shield, butterfly hooks, or other leg-based defensive structures.

This position represents a transitional control point in modern BJJ guard passing systems, bridging the gap between initial guard engagement and final passing positions like side control or mount. The leg weave allows the top player to systematically dismantle the bottom player's defensive frames while maintaining forward pressure and control. The position is characterized by the top player's leg creating a "weave" pattern through the opponent's guard, hence the name.

Mastery of the leg weave position requires precise weight distribution, understanding of angles, and the ability to chain multiple passing sequences together. Elite practitioners use this position to create passing dilemmas where the bottom player must choose between defending different passing threats, often leading to successful guard passes with high percentage rates at advanced levels.
state_invariants: Top player's lead leg is threaded between bottom player's legs, creating a weaving pattern that disrupts defensive leg positioning and prevents the bottom player from establishing effective guard retention frames

Upper body control maintained through grips on the opponent's collar, sleeves, or underhooks, with the top player's chest pressure directed toward the bottom player's upper body to prevent them from sitting up or creating distance

Bottom player on their back or side with limited ability to establish butterfly hooks, knee shield, or other leg-based defensive structures due to the top player's leg positioning disrupting their base and frame

Top player's hips positioned forward and low, creating constant forward pressure that drives through the bottom player's center line while maintaining balance and preventing the bottom player from recovering guard or sweeping

Weight distribution favoring the lead leg side, with the top player's base controlled through their non-weaving leg and hands, creating a stable platform that allows for dynamic passing movements while maintaining pressure
prerequisites: Initial guard engagement from standing or combat base position
Successful opening of closed guard or engagement with open guard variations
Control of at least one upper body grip (collar, sleeve, or underhook)
Bottom player unable to establish effective knee shield or butterfly hook retention
Top player's posture and base stable enough to thread leg without being swept
key_principles: Thread the lead leg deep between opponent's legs while maintaining upper body connection and forward pressure
Keep hips low and driving forward to prevent bottom player from creating space or recovering guard
Control opponent's upper body with grips or underhooks to prevent them from sitting up or framing effectively
Use the weaved leg to pin opponent's bottom leg while freeing the top leg for passing
Maintain constant pressure and angle changes to prevent bottom player from establishing defensive frames
Chain multiple passing threats together to create dilemmas for the bottom player
Keep weight distributed between the weaved leg and supporting leg to maintain balance and prevent sweeps

counter_transitions.trigger: Opponent attempts to recover knee shield or create frames
Opponent turns away or attempts to turtle
Opponent flattens out and tries to prevent pass with legs
Opponent exposes back while attempting deep half entry

decision_tree.condition: If opponent attempts to create frames with arms or recover knee shield position
If opponent turns away or attempts to come up to turtle position
If opponent flattens out completely and attempts to use leg positioning to prevent pass
If opponent attempts deep half guard entry or underhook sweep

common_errors.error: Threading leg too shallow between opponent's legs without deep penetration
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can easily recover knee shield or butterfly hooks, negating the leg weave control
common_errors.correction: Drive the lead leg deep between opponent's legs until your knee is past their hip line, ensuring maximum disruption of their defensive structure

common_errors.error: Allowing hips to rise too high or losing forward pressure during the weave
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player creates space to recover guard or sit up, losing passing momentum
common_errors.correction: Keep hips low and constantly driving forward with chest pressure directed at opponent's upper body throughout the passing sequence

common_errors.error: Neglecting upper body control while focusing solely on leg positioning
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player sits up, frames effectively, or creates angles that allow guard recovery
common_errors.correction: Maintain at least one strong upper body grip (collar, sleeve, or underhook) while threading the leg, using upper body control to prevent opponent from sitting up

common_errors.error: Committing too much weight to the weaved leg, losing balance and base
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player can execute sweeps or recover guard by attacking the top player's compromised balance
common_errors.correction: Distribute weight between weaved leg, supporting leg, and hands to maintain a stable base while applying pressure

common_errors.error: Staying static in the leg weave position without chaining passing sequences
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player adjusts to the position and finds defensive solutions or escape routes
common_errors.correction: Continuously threaten multiple passing directions (knee slice, leg drag, smash pass) to create dilemmas and prevent the bottom player from settling into defensive postures

common_errors.error: Ignoring opponent's underhook attempts during the leg weave
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player establishes deep underhook that enables sweeps or deep half guard entries
common_errors.correction: Immediately address underhook attempts by crossfacing, posting the arm, or switching to alternative passing angles that neutralize the underhook threat

expert_insights.danaher: The leg weave represents a sophisticated passing mechanism that exploits fundamental principles of base disruption and frame negation. When you thread your leg between the opponent's legs, you're systematically destroying their ability to create the leg-based frames that are essential to modern guard retention. The key is understanding that this is not merely a leg position, but a complete control system. Your weaved leg must pin their bottom leg while your upper body controls prevent them from sitting up. The biomechanics demand that you maintain constant forward pressure with your hips while using your grips to control their upper body rotation. This creates a situation where the bottom player cannot effectively use their legs for framing or their upper body for posture recovery. The position becomes exponentially more powerful when you understand it as a platform for creating passing dilemmas rather than a singular passing technique. By threatening knee slice, leg drag, and smash pass simultaneously, you force the opponent into defensive choices that inevitably open passing lanes.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the leg weave is one of my highest percentage passing positions because it completely shuts down modern guard retention systems that rely on leg-based frames. When I get my leg threaded deep between their legs, I'm immediately looking to chain passes together - if they defend the knee slice, I'm going to the leg drag; if they defend the leg drag, I'm smashing through or taking the back. The position works so well because most people train guard retention based on keeping the passer at distance with knee shields and butterfly hooks, but the leg weave destroys those frames before they can even establish them. What makes this position elite-level is that you're not just passing - you're controlling the pace and creating situations where every defensive movement opens up a different passing opportunity. Against high-level opponents, I'm constantly adjusting my pressure and grips to keep them guessing which pass is coming. The leg weave gives me that control and those options, which is why it's a fundamental part of my no-gi passing system.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The leg weave is sick for no-gi because it takes away all those annoying leg frames that people use to stall out guard passing. When you thread that leg deep, you're basically telling their legs 'you don't work anymore' and then it's game over for their guard. I teach my guys to think of it as creating a highway to the pass - once your leg is woven in, you've got a straight shot to side control or the back depending on how they react. The beauty of this position is that it works perfectly with the modern leg lock game too. If they try to enter on your legs while you're in the leg weave, you're already in perfect position to counter with leg entanglements or take their back. What's really innovative about the leg weave is how it bridges old school pressure passing with new school leg lock systems. You can use it to pass traditionally, or you can use it as an entry point into the saddle or other leg attack positions. That versatility makes it essential for the complete modern grappler who needs to threaten both positional dominance and leg attacks.
